A_target.statement:
For [[Definition:Square-Integrable Random Variable|square-integrable]] random variables, [[Definition:Covariance|covariance]] is symmetric and bilinear, and:
:$\var {a X + b Y} = a^2 \var X + 2 a b \cov {X, Y} + b^2 \var Y$
:$\displaystyle \var {\sum_i X_i} = \sum_{i, j} \cov {X_i, X_j}$
Moreover $\var X = 0$ {{iff}} $X$ is [[Definition:Almost Surely|almost surely]] constant.

B_source.statement:
$\innerprod U V = \expect {U V}$ is an [[Definition:Inner Product|inner product]] on $\map {L^2} \Pr$, and:
:$
orm {u + v}^2 = 
orm u^2 + 2 \innerprod u v + 
orm v^2$

derived.the polarization expansion: the variance of a linear combination

object_map.reformulation: Transport the inner product along the linear centring map, so that covariance becomes an inner product on random variables modulo constants.

validity_conditions: Centring X -> X - E[X] is linear, so the pulled-back form is bilinear.
Its kernel consists of the almost surely constant variables, so covariance is an inner product only modulo constants.
proof_plan:
Let $\map c X = X - \expect X$, a linear map on $\map {L^2} \Pr$.
Then $\cov {X, Y} = \innerprod {\map c X} {\map c Y}$ and $\var X = \norm {\map c X}^2$.
The pullback of a symmetric bilinear form along a linear map is symmetric bilinear, so covariance is symmetric and bilinear.
Applying the source expansion to $\map c {a X + b Y} = a \map c X + b \map c Y$ gives the variance formula; induction gives the formula for sums.

$\var X = 0$ {{iff}} $\map c X = 0$ in $\map {L^2} \Pr$, that is, $X = \expect X$ almost surely.
{{qed}}
